title: Sun, stand still (Joshua 10:12–14)
hookLine: Joshua asks the sun to stand still at Gibeon

lines: A NIGHT MARCH TO SAVE THEM.
cards: A messenger runs into the camp at Gilgal. Gibeon is surrounded. The kings of the region have joined forces against the city, because it made peace with Israel.
Gibeon's message is short: don't abandon your servants; come quickly and save us. These are the same people who walked in with moldy bread and a lie. Joshua could let the treaty quietly fail.
Instead he marches his army through the whole night, uphill, and falls on the attackers suddenly. And in the middle of that long day, he says something to the sky.

teach.h: AN OLD SONG, SUN AND MOON.
teach.b: His words: "Sun, stand thou still upon Gibeon," and you, moon, in the valley of Aijalon. And the sun stood, and the moon stayed, until the people had won the day.
Notice the shape: it's poetry, two lines that echo each other, sun and moon, Gibeon and Aijalon.
And the text says where it comes from: the book of Jashar, a book the Bible names but doesn't include. So this is an old song, quoted in the middle of the story. Now one word.
The Hebrew for stand still is dom. In the Psalms the same word means be still, be silent. A reader can hear Joshua telling the sun, hush.
Wait. Not yet. What happened in the sky?
Jewish readers differ, and the tradition keeps both. Some take it as it sounds, a wonder in the heavens.
Some medieval commentators, Gersonides among them, read it another way: the light held long enough, the battle ended before the sun went down, and that was the wonder. Then read the next verse.
When the text marvels at this day, it doesn't marvel at the sun. It says there was no day like it, before or after, "that the LORD hearkened unto the voice of a man." The surprise isn't astronomy.
A person spoke, in the middle of keeping a hard promise, and God listened.

how: Jewish commentators read Joshua 10:12–14 in different ways, from a miracle in the heavens to a battle that ended before nightfall, and the passage is studied as part of the Former Prophets.

games.q: you're Joshua. a messenger says Gibeon is surrounded, the city that tricked you into a treaty. what do you do?
o: let the attackers settle it: the treaty was a trick.
march all night to defend them.
send a few men and keep the army home.
games.why: Joshua marches through the whole night from Gilgal and falls on the attackers suddenly. the oath he was tricked into, he keeps with his army.

practice: Put the phone face down or out of reach, and let your breathing slow on its own.
Look at the light in the room or outside, where it falls, how bright it is, and let the day stand still around you, with nothing to finish and nothing to win.
If a thought pulls you toward the next thing, tell it quietly, the way Joshua spoke to the sun: hush, not yet.

wordCard.voice: Sun. The sun Joshua told to stand still over Gibeon, in an old song from the book of Jashar, on a day God listened to a person. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: be still, be silent. Joshua's word to the sun.

carryVoice: Your line: hush, not yet. The day can wait a moment while you listen. See you tomorrow.
